titulo: How many people for two to share a birthday?
fuentes: Wikipedia, 'Birthday problem': 23 people about 50.7%; 40 people about 89.1%; 70 people about 99.9% (365 equally likely days)
Wolfram MathWorld, 'Birthday Problem': 23 people 0.507297; non-uniform birthdays
Birthdays are not evenly spread through the year; any non-uniform distribution makes a match more likely, not less (Wikipedia, 'Birthday problem')
destinatario: se lo manda un amigo de grupo a otro que jura que nadie en su grupo cumple el mismo día, para desafiarlo a chequear
receta: A vs B con cuenta a la vista (pares)

frases.texto: You think two people sharing a birthday takes a huge crowd.
frases.estilo: Dry and confident, with a half smile.

frases.texto: With twenty-three people, the odds of a shared birthday are already over fifty percent.
The trick: it's not the people that count, it's the pairs.
frases.estilo: Explaining simply, like to a friend.

frases.texto: Twenty-three people make two hundred fifty-three pairs, and every pair is a chance to match.
Forty people? About ninety percent. Seventy? Over ninety-nine.
Heads up: the math assumes every day is equally likely. Real birthdays aren't, which nudges the odds up a bit.
And it doesn't have to be your birthday. Any two people in the room count.
At your next party of twenty-three or more, ask around.
Send this to the friend who swears nobody in their group shares a birthday.
frases.estilo: Playful, with humor, as a punchline.
